title: Section 1.7: Solving Linear Equations with Fractions — Clearing the LCD
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 13 • Section 1.7 (Workbook p. 20)
detail: Lecture 13: Solving Linear Equations with Fractions (The LCD Clearing Method)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### The Golden Clearing Fractions Strategy (Workbook p. 20)
$$\text{Reminder: Whatever you do to one side, you MUST do to the other side!}$$
- **Instead of struggling with fraction arithmetic**, multiply **EVERY SINGLE TERM on both sides by the LCD**!
- All denominators will cancel out into whole integers in one single step!
- **Key equivalence:** $\frac{3}{4}x = \frac{3x}{4}$.
pitfall: **Sora's Warning:** You must multiply EVERY term by the LCD, including standalone integers with no denominator!
script:
[Prof. Park] Welcome everyone to Lecture 13 of M090 Introductory Algebra! I am Professor Eunju Park, and joining me at the teaching desk is TA Sora.

[TA Sora] Today, we dive into Section 1.7 of our course workbook, found on pages 20 through 22: Solving Linear Equations with Fractions by Clearing the LCD. Hello everyone!

[Prof. Park] If you ask algebra students across the country what topic stresses them out the most, a huge percentage will immediately say: 'Fractions in equations!' Fractions make people nervous because finding common denominators and adding fractions at every single step of an equation is tedious and prone to arithmetic mistakes.

[TA Sora] Well, today, we have the best news of the entire semester: You do NOT have to do fraction arithmetic when solving an equation! You can completely ELIMINATE all fractions in one single, glorious opening step!

[Prof. Park] That is the power of the 'Clearing Fractions Strategy.' Remember our Golden Rule of Equality: Whatever you do to one side of an equation, you must do to the other side.

[TA Sora] If you multiply BOTH sides of an equation by the Least Common Denominator (LCD) of ALL fractions in the equation, every single denominator divides evenly into that LCD and cancels out into whole integers! Your ugly fraction equation instantly transforms into a friendly, whole-number equation from Lecture 11!

[Prof. Park] Notice the huge difference between Section 1.5 and Section 1.7: In Section 1.5, we had an EXPRESSION (like 1/2 x + 3/4). There was no equal sign, so we could NOT eliminate denominatorsâwe had to keep the LCD!

[TA Sora] In Section 1.7, we have an EQUATION with an equal sign! Because there is an equal sign, we can multiply both sides by the LCD and completely vaporize the denominators! Also remember the key equivalence: (3/4)x is identically equal to (3x)/4.

[Prof. Park] The x can sit next to the fraction or upstairs in the numerator, but NEVER in the denominator! Let's see this in action on slide 2!

[TA Sora] In physics and engineering research at Montana State University, mathematical models of fluid dynamics, aerodynamics, and circuit resistance routinely generate complex equations filled with rational coefficients.

[Prof. Park] Senior engineering professors don't crunch fractions by hand across twenty lines of paperâthey immediately clear denominators by multiplying through by the system's common modulus! What you are learning today in Section 1.7 is the exact industry-standard simplification algorithm used by professional engineers and scientific software.

[TA Sora] And notice the emotional shift when you learn this technique: Students go from dreading fraction problems to being excited when they see one on a quiz, because clearing fractions feels like magic! With one stroke of your pen, every fraction vanishes, leaving a simple integer puzzle.

title: Example 1 & 2: Dividing by Coefficient vs. Clearing LCD
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 13 • Section 1.7 Example 1 & 2 (Workbook p. 20)
detail: Lecture 13: Solving Linear Equations with Fractions (The LCD Clearing Method)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Two Methods for the Same Equation (Workbook p. 20)
$$\frac{3}{4}x = 15$$
- **Example 1:** Solve by dividing both sides by the coefficient (multiplying by reciprocal $\frac{4}{3}$).
- **Example 2:** Solve by the method of clearing fractions (multiplying both sides by LCD $= 4$).
pitfall: **Both yield 20!** Notice how Method 2 eliminates the fraction immediately, converting it into $3x = 60$.
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 2, let's compare two different methods for solving the exact same equation from workbook page 20: (3/4)x = 15. Method 1 (Dividing by the Coefficient): x is multiplied by the fraction 3/4.

[TA Sora] To undo multiplying by 3/4, we multiply both sides by its reciprocal: 4/3! (4/3) Â· (3/4)x = (4/3) Â· 15. On the left: (4/3)(3/4) = 12/12 = 1, leaving x. On the right: (4/3) Â· (15/1) = (4 Â· 15) / 3 = 60 / 3 = 20!

[Prof. Park] So x = 20. That works very nicely when there is only one single term on each side. Now let's look at Method 2: The Method of Clearing Fractions! The only denominator in the equation is 4, so our LCD is 4.

[TA Sora] Multiply BOTH sides of the equation by 4: 4 Â· [ (3/4)x ] = 4 Â· [ 15 ]. On the left side: the 4 in front cancels the 4 in the denominator: 4 Â· (3/4) = 3! Leaving: 3x.

[Prof. Park] On the right side: 4 Â· 15 = 60! Now we have the simplest one-step equation imaginable: 3x = 60! Divide both sides by 3: x = 60 / 3 = 20! Notice how much easier Method 2 is when equations get longer!

[TA Sora] Instead of carrying fractions through multiple steps, you multiply by 4 on step 1, and you're dealing with clean, easy whole numbers: 3x = 60, x = 20. Method 2 is our standard protocol for the rest of this chapter!

[Prof. Park] Let's emphasize why Method 1 (multiplying by the reciprocal) is only useful for single-term equations: If you have (3/4)x = 15, multiplying by 4/3 is great. But if you have (3/4)x + 2/5 = 7/10, what would you multiply by?

[TA Sora] You can't multiply by the reciprocal of 3/4 without turning the other terms into horrific fractions! That is why Method 2âclearing fractions using the LCDâis universally superior for general equations! Method 2 works on ALL equations, whether they have one term, three terms, or ten terms!

[Prof. Park] Always master the universal method that never lets you down.

title: Example 3A & 3B: Simple Fraction Equations
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 13 • Section 1.7 Example 3A & 3B (Workbook p. 20)
detail: Lecture 13: Solving Linear Equations with Fractions (The LCD Clearing Method)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Use the method of clearing fractions to solve (Workbook p. 20)
$$\text{A. } \frac{x}{-5} = 10$$
$$\text{B. } \frac{1}{2}y + \frac{3}{4} = 10$$
pitfall: **Don't forget the standalone 10!** In 3B, $4 \cdot 10 = 40$. A common mistake is writing $2y + 3 = 10$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 3 presents Section 1.7 Examples 3A and 3B from workbook page 20: Example 3A: x / (-5) = 10. Example 3B: (1/2)y + 3/4 = 10. In Example 3A: x / (-5) = 10. x is divided by -5. The denominator is -5.

[TA Sora] To clear the denominator, multiply both sides by -5: (-5) Â· [ x / (-5) ] = (-5) Â· [ 10 ]. On the left, -5 cancels -5, leaving x. On the right: (-5)(10) = -50! So x = -50. Check: -50 / -5 = +10. Perfect!

[Prof. Park] Now look at Example 3B: (1/2)y + 3/4 = 10. Notice there are THREE terms in this equation: (1/2)y, +3/4, and 10! The denominators are 2 and 4. What is the LCD of 2 and 4? It is 4! Now listen carefully to Sora's Golden Warning:
Golden Warning!

[TA Sora] When you clear fractions, you must multiply EVERY SINGLE TERM on both sides by the LCDâeven terms that are NOT fractions! The number 10 on the right side does NOT have a fraction, but it MUST still be multiplied by 4!

[Prof. Park] If you multiply the left side by 4 and forget to multiply the 10 by 4, your scale will tip and your answer will be totally wrong!

[TA Sora] Let's multiply every term by 4: 4 Â· [ (1/2)y ] + 4 Â· [ 3/4 ] = 4 Â· [ 10 ]. First term: 4 Â· (1/2) = 2, so we get 2y. Second term: 4 Â· (3/4) = 3, so we get +3.

[Prof. Park] Third term: 4 Â· 10 = 40! Look at our new equation: 2y + 3 = 40! All fractions are gone! Now solve: subtract 3 from both sides: 2y = 40 - 3 = 37. Divide by 2: y = 37/2! Clean, elegant, and solved in seconds!

[TA Sora] Let's do another sanity check on Example 3B: (1/2)y + 3/4 = 10. We found y = 37/2. Let's plug it back into the original fraction equation to verify: (1/2)(37/2) + 3/4 = 37/4 + 3/4 = 40/4 = 10! 10 = 10!

[Prof. Park] The verification took ten seconds and proves our answer is rock solid! And remember Sora's Golden Warning: The integer 10 had to be multiplied by 4 to become 40.

[TA Sora] Think of distributing the LCD like distributing hot chocolate to campers around a campfire: You can't skip the camper sitting on the right just because they didn't bring a fraction cup! Every single term gets a cup of LCD!

title: Example 3C & 3D: Multi-Denominator Clearing
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 13 • Section 1.7 Example 3C & 3D (Workbook p. 21)
detail: Lecture 13: Solving Linear Equations with Fractions (The LCD Clearing Method)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Use clearing fractions to solve (Workbook p. 21)
$$\text{C. } \frac{1}{2}x - \frac{2}{7} = \frac{5}{4} - x$$
$$\text{D. } \frac{3}{5} + \frac{x}{5} = 18$$
pitfall: **Multiplying Variables:** In 3C, $-x$ must also be multiplied by 28, becoming $-28x$!
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 4, we examine Section 1.7 Examples 3C and 3D from workbook page 21: Example 3C: (1/2)x - 2/7 = 5/4 - x. Example 3D: 3/5 + x/5 = 18. Let's analyze Example 3C: (1/2)x - 2/7 = 5/4 - x.

[TA Sora] Look at the denominators: 2, 7, and 4. What is the LCD of 2, 7, and 4? Between 2 and 4, the LCM is 4. Between 4 and 7, they share no common factors, so 4 Â· 7 = 28! Our LCD is 28!

[Prof. Park] Now, multiply EVERY SINGLE TERM by 28: 28 Â· [ (1/2)x ] - 28 Â· [ 2/7 ] = 28 Â· [ 5/4 ] - 28 Â· [ x ]. Let's simplify each product carefully: First term: 28 / 2 = 14, so 14x.

[TA Sora] Second term: 28 / 7 = 4, and 4 Â· 2 = 8, so -8. Third term: 28 / 4 = 7, and 7 Â· 5 = 35, so 35. Fourth term: 28 Â· x = 28x, so -28x.

[Prof. Park] Our equation is now: 14x - 8 = 35 - 28x! That is wonderful! Add 28x to both sides: 14x + 28x - 8 = 35, which gives 42x - 8 = 35. Add 8 to both sides: 42x = 35 + 8 = 43.

[TA Sora] Divide both sides by 42: x = 43/42! Imagine how messy that would have been if you tried to find common denominators and add fractions across the equal sign four times! Clearing fractions with LCD = 28 made it effortless.

[Prof. Park] Now look at Example 3D: 3/5 + x/5 = 18. The denominator is 5. Multiply every term by 5: 5 Â· (3/5) + 5 Â· (x/5) = 5 Â· (18). 3 + x = 90! Subtract 3 from both sides: x = 90 - 3 = 87! Done!

[TA Sora] In Example 3C, our denominators were 2, 7, and 4. Let's review how we found LCD = 28 using prime factorization: 2 is prime: 2^1. 7 is prime: 7^1. 4 is 2^2.

[Prof. Park] To build the LCD, we take the highest power of every prime factor: Highest power of 2 is 2^2 = 4. Highest power of 7 is 7^1 = 7. 4 Â· 7 = 28!

[TA Sora] Prime factorization takes the guesswork out of finding the LCD, no matter how complicated the numbers are! And notice how cleanly 28 divided into every denominator: 28/2 = 14. 28/7 = 4. 28/4 = 7.

[Prof. Park] If your LCD doesn't divide evenly into every denominator, you made a mistake finding the LCD! The whole point of the LCD is that every denominator cancels into a whole integer.

title: Example 3E: Clearing Fractions with Parentheses
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 13 • Section 1.7 Example 3E (Workbook p. 21)
detail: Lecture 13: Solving Linear Equations with Fractions (The LCD Clearing Method)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Use clearing fractions to solve (Workbook p. 21)
$$\frac{1}{7}(x - 4) + 5 = \frac{1}{2}(3x + 4)$$
pitfall: **Multiplying Terms with Parentheses:** In $14 \cdot \frac{1}{7}(x - 4)$, the 14 only multiplies the fraction $\frac{1}{7}$ to make 2! Do NOT multiply inside the parentheses yet!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 5 presents Section 1.7 Example 3E on workbook page 21: Clearing Fractions when Parentheses are Present: (1/7)(x - 4) + 5 = (1/2)(3x + 4). Warning! Look at the expression (1/7)(x - 4). Is (x - 4) a separate term?

[TA Sora] NO! (1/7)(x - 4) is ONE SINGLE TERM because 1/7 is multiplied by (x - 4)! When you multiply this term by the LCD, you multiply the fraction 1/7 in FRONT of the parentheses! Do NOT multiply inside the parentheses yet! That is such a crucial distinction.

[Prof. Park] The denominators are 7 and 2. The LCD of 7 and 2 is 14. Let's multiply every term by 14: 14 Â· [ (1/7)(x - 4) ] + 14 Â· [ 5 ] = 14 Â· [ (1/2)(3x + 4) ].

[TA Sora] Look at the first term: 14 Â· (1/7) = 2! So it becomes: 2(x - 4). Second term: 14 Â· 5 = 70. Right side: 14 Â· (1/2) = 7! So it becomes: 7(3x + 4).

[Prof. Park] Our equation is now: 2(x - 4) + 70 = 7(3x + 4)! Look how clean that is! All fractions are gone, and now we just use our standard distribution from Lecture 11: Left: 2x - 8 + 70 = 2x + 62. Right: 21x + 28.

[TA Sora] So we have: 2x + 62 = 21x + 28. Subtract 2x from both sides: 62 = 19x + 28. Subtract 28 from both sides: 34 = 19x. Divide by 19: x = 34/19! What a magnificent, orderly solution!

[Prof. Park] On slide 5, let's revisit why we did NOT multiply inside the parentheses: In (1/7)(x - 4), think of (x - 4) as a locked suitcase, and 1/7 is the luggage tag on the handle.

[TA Sora] When the airport scanner (14) multiplies the bag, it only multiplies the tag on the outside: 14 Â· (1/7) = 2! The suitcase (x - 4) remains safely locked until the next step!

[Prof. Park] Multiplying both the outside and inside would be multiplying by 14 TWICE (which would be multiplying by 196)! That suitcase analogy is unforgettable! Only multiply the outside coefficient factor by the LCD.

title: Example 3F & 3G: Fractional Proportions & Compound Terms
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 13 • Section 1.7 Example 3F & 3G (Workbook p. 22)
detail: Lecture 13: Solving Linear Equations with Fractions (The LCD Clearing Method)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Use clearing fractions to solve (Workbook p. 22)
$$\text{F. } \frac{x - 7}{8} = \frac{5}{6}$$
$$\text{G. } \frac{1}{3}(3m + 1) = \frac{1}{4}(m - 4) + 1$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ F:}\quad & \text{LCD of } 8 \text{ and } 6 \text{ is } 24. \\
& 24 \cdot \left(\frac{x - 7}{8}\right) = 24 \cdot \left(\frac{5}{6}\right) \\
& 3(x - 7) = 4(5) \implies 3x - 21 = 20 \\
& 3x = 41 \implies \mathbf{x = \frac{41}{3}} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ G:}\quad & \text{LCD of } 3 \text{ and } 4 \text{ is } 12. \\
& 12 \cdot \left[\frac{1}{3}(3m + 1)\right] = 12 \cdot \left[\frac{1}{4}(m - 4)\right] + 12 \cdot (1) \\
& 4(3m + 1) = 3(m - 4) + 12 \\
& 12m + 4 = 3m - 12 + 12 \implies 12m + 4 = 3m \\
& 9m = -4 \implies \mathbf{m = -\frac{4}{9}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Don't forget the +1 in 3G:** $12 \cdot 1 = 12$. Notice on the right side: $-12 + 12 = 0$, leaving just $3m$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 6 concludes Lecture 13 with Section 1.7 Examples 3F and 3G from workbook page 22: Example 3F: (x - 7) / 8 = 5/6. Example 3G: (1/3)(3m + 1) = (1/4)(m - 4) + 1. Let's look at Example 3F: (x - 7) / 8 = 5/6.

[TA Sora] This is a single fraction equal to a single fractionâa proportion! The denominators are 8 and 6. The LCD of 8 and 6 is 24! Multiply both sides by 24: 24 Â· [ (x - 7) / 8 ] = 24 Â· [ 5/6 ].

[Prof. Park] On the left: 24 / 8 = 3, so we have: 3(x - 7). On the right: 24 / 6 = 4, and 4 Â· 5 = 20! So our equation is: 3(x - 7) = 20. Distribute: 3x - 21 = 20.

[TA Sora] Add 21 to both sides: 3x = 41. Divide by 3: x = 41/3! Now let's solve Example 3G: (1/3)(3m + 1) = (1/4)(m - 4) + 1. Denominators are 3 and 4, so the LCD is 12!

[Prof. Park] Multiply EVERY term by 12: 12 Â· [ (1/3)(3m + 1) ] = 12 Â· [ (1/4)(m - 4) ] + 12 Â· [ 1 ]. Left: 12 Â· (1/3) = 4, so: 4(3m + 1). Right first term: 12 Â· (1/4) = 3, so: 3(m - 4).

[TA Sora] Right second term: 12 Â· 1 = 12. So we have: 4(3m + 1) = 3(m - 4) + 12. Distribute: 12m + 4 = 3m - 12 + 12. -12 + 12 = 0, so: 12m + 4 = 3m.

[Prof. Park] Subtract 12m from both sides: 4 = -9m. Divide by -9: m = -4/9! That concludes Section 1.7! In Lecture 14, we will master Section 1.8: Solving Formulas for a Specified Variable. Great job everyone, and we will see you in Lecture 14!

[TA Sora] In Example 3F, (x - 7)/8 = 5/6, many high school students are taught 'cross-multiplication': 6(x - 7) = 8 Â· 5 = 40. Notice that 6(x - 7) = 40 is 6x - 42 = 40, 6x = 82, x = 82/6 = 41/3!

[Prof. Park] Cross-multiplication gives the exact same result, but it uses the common denominator 48 instead of the LEAST common denominator 24! Using LCD = 24 kept our numbers smaller (3x - 21 = 20) and prevented awkward reduction at the end!

[TA Sora] Clearing by LCD is the master technique that generalizes to all rational equations in college algebra!
